claims.text: An integrated EMTO-CPA DFT and CALPHAD framework can predict melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, volume change on melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties of high-entropy alloys.
The integrated framework is more accurate than standalone CALPHAD or lower-level DFT.
The integrated framework is more efficient than traditional methods.
The representative initial state is a near-melting random solid solution.
EMTO-CPA DFT can account for finite-temperature electronic, magnetic, and phononic free-energy contributions.
CALPHAD can efficiently determine multicomponent phase behavior using Gibbs free energies and related thermodynamic data.
CALPHAD can extrapolate detailed EMTO-CPA DFT inputs across multicomponent composition space.
The intended application conditions are equilibrium or quasi-equilibrium near melting for predominantly FCC or similar random solid solutions.
Near-melting phase stability is mediated by the balance between configurational entropy and enthalpy.
EMTO-CPA DFT accurately models short-range contributions to free energy near melting.
EMTO-CPA DFT models thermal electronic, magnetic, and phononic contributions to free energy.
CALPHAD maps detailed electronic-structure inputs onto broader phase equilibria.
Combining EMTO-CPA DFT with CALPHAD yields more reliable melting and liquid-phase predictions than either method alone.
Predicted fusion parameters will deviate from calorimetric and dilatometric measurements by approximately 5–10%.
Standalone CALPHAD and lower-level DFT generally require empirical adjustments or have larger uncertainty because they oversimplify entropy contributions.
The approach should perform best for predominantly disordered high-entropy solid solutions near melting.
Strong local short-range order or atypical electron-phonon interactions may reduce predictive performance.
Complex local ordering and substantial nonideal mixing may produce larger errors through limitations in DFT or CALPHAD approximations.
DSC and high-temperature dilatometry can measure the melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, derived fusion entropy, and volume change needed to validate the model.
Systematic deviations greater than approximately 15% for a majority of tested compositions would falsify the approach.
